# Methods

## Set-up

Only one of the three canals built in the system was used. Prior to the experiments, the lower and upper tanks were slightly modified by installing a metal plate to direct the flow of the lower valve towards the rank. Additionally, possible escape routes from the test tank were closed with a small mesh sized grid (mesh size = ???). Potential “shelter” areas under the bottom plates of the valve were also closed off. Deceased fish were additionally observed on the lower antenna, resulting from the “green grid” being lifted and lowered. The grid was as such removed from ??? date onwards. 

Two HDX PIT antennae (40 mm * 50 mm) made of copper coil wrapped around graphite bars and connected to permanent readers were installed, each on the front of the upper or lower valve. They were both tuned to have a narrow detection range of approximately 15 cm maximum so that fish would be detected when they cross the valve only – and thus enter the system. Preliminary testing of the system was conducted, assuring the efficiency and detection range of the PIT telemetry set-up. 

## Data processing

All the different sites were fish were either released, detected or recaptured are further one referred to as nodes. 

Pit tag data was compressed using the default settings of the function compress of the R package PITCleanr. This data compression involves determining the first and last detection of a series of subsequent detections on a node as well as the number of detections during each slot (from first and last detection). For fish being detected on several nodes, 

The location where the fish were released was designated as the initial node, with the corresponding timestamp marking the start of each fish's journey. Conversely, the recapture location was identified as the final node, with the corresponding timestamp indicating the end of each fish's journey. All fish were alive and presumed to still have their tags at the time of release. However, some fish were found dead and/or tagless upon recapture. Due to the low detection rate of the antennas, particularly the upper one, we did not attempt to match unidentified fish with tag IDs from the release data. In a system with higher detectability, it might have been feasible to trace unidentified fish back to known but not-recaptured tag IDs with a reasonable degree of certainty. Unfortunately, this was not the case in our system. To prevent artificial inflation of the number of fish entering the experiment, fish found without a tag in the basin below were excluded from the dataset. For instance, an unidentified fish with a new ID (e.g., unknown_4) would also have had a real ID. Including this fish in the data would have resulted in double-counting. However, fish found without a tag in other locations were still included in the dataset, as there was no risk of double-counting once they had moved away from their initial node.

The temporal resolution and range of the valve-opening and pressure data was different between experiments. In order to harmonize the temporal resolution between experiments and to easily link fish data with valve and pressure data, linear interpolation was applied to yield a temporal resolution of one second. A valve was considered open when the opening was larger than 25 cm. For every second the time since the last opening was determined. 

Time was for all data initially in local Brussels time but was changed to UTC for transparancy.
